security_audit.summary: I found no evidence of hidden exfiltration, prompt injection, or malicious payloads in the reviewed files. Most static detections are Markdown examples or placeholders; the real issue is an evaluation harness that can launch user-selected MCP servers and forward user-provided secrets. Users should run it only with trusted commands, URLs, and credentials.

remediation.issue: Evaluation harness can run user-selected local commands.
remediation.suggestion: Document that users must run only trusted MCP servers and review command arguments before execution.

remediation.issue: Examples show secrets passed on the command line.
remediation.suggestion: Prefer environment setup outside shell history and warn users not to paste real tokens into shared commands.

remediation.issue: Remote transports accept arbitrary URLs and headers.
remediation.suggestion: Warn users to verify remote MCP endpoints before sending authorization headers or other credentials.

semantic_findings.title: User-Controlled MCP Server Execution
semantic_findings.description: The evaluation CLI accepts command, args, environment variables, URL, and headers, then creates an MCP connection. This is expected for testing, but untrusted values can execute local programs or send credentials to remote servers.
semantic_findings.confidence_reasoning: The CLI arguments are explicitly wired into create_connection and then into stdio_client or remote clients. The risk depends on user-supplied targets, so severity is medium rather than high.

content.value_statement: MCP server projects need clear tool design, safe integrations, and realistic testing. This skill guides planning, implementation, and evaluation for Python and TypeScript servers.
actual_capabilities: Guides MCP server planning around workflows instead of raw API endpoints.
Covers Python FastMCP and Node/TypeScript SDK implementation patterns.
Explains tool schemas, annotations, pagination, response formats, and error handling.
Provides reference material for MCP best practices and language-specific examples.
Includes an evaluation harness for XML question and answer test sets.
limitations: It does not provide a finished MCP server for a specific service.
External API documentation must still be reviewed for each integration.
The evaluation harness requires Anthropic credentials and MCP dependencies.
Local commands, remote URLs, headers, and credentials need user security review.

use_cases.title: Plan a New Integration
use_cases.description: Map an external service into a focused MCP tool set with validation, pagination, and useful response formats.

use_cases.title: Improve Tool Quality
use_cases.description: Review an MCP server for naming, annotations, concise outputs, error handling, and agent-friendly workflows.

use_cases.title: Evaluate Server Usefulness
use_cases.description: Create realistic read-only evaluation questions and run them through the included MCP evaluation harness.

prompt_templates.title: Choose Server Scope
prompt_templates.prompt: Help me plan an MCP server for [service]. Identify the most valuable workflows, required API docs, and the first five tools.

prompt_templates.title: Design Tool Contracts
prompt_templates.prompt: Design MCP tool names, inputs, response formats, annotations, and error messages for these workflows: [workflow list].

prompt_templates.title: Review Existing Server
prompt_templates.prompt: Review this MCP server for tool design, validation, pagination, response size limits, security checks, and agent usability.

prompt_templates.title: Build Evaluation Suite
prompt_templates.prompt: Create a read-only evaluation plan for this MCP server. Include realistic questions, verification steps, and expected answer constraints.

output_examples.input: Plan an MCP server for a support ticketing API.
output: Prioritized workflows for ticket search, triage, assignment, and status reporting.
Recommended tools with clear names, input constraints, and concise response formats.
Authentication, pagination, rate-limit, and error-handling notes for implementation.

output_examples.input: Review a TypeScript MCP server before release.
output: A checklist covering strict types, Zod schemas, annotations, build output, and response limits.
Findings about unclear tool descriptions, missing pagination, weak errors, or unsafe defaults.
Concrete remediation steps ordered by release risk.

output_examples.input: Create evaluations for an MCP server.
output: Ten stable, read-only questions that require multiple tool calls.
Expected answers with verification notes and removal guidance for destructive tasks.
Instructions for running the evaluation harness and reviewing accuracy reports.

best_practices: Start from user workflows, then choose the smallest tool set that completes them.
Use strict validation, clear annotations, concise outputs, and actionable error messages.
Test with realistic read-only evaluations before expanding tool coverage.
anti_patterns: Do not wrap every API endpoint as a separate MCP tool without workflow design.
Do not return large raw payloads when summaries or pagination would work better.
Do not run untrusted MCP servers, URLs, headers, or credentials through the harness.

faq.question: What does this skill help build?
faq.answer: It helps build Model Context Protocol servers that expose external services through useful AI agent tools.

faq.question: Which languages does it cover?
faq.answer: It covers Python with FastMCP and Node or TypeScript with the MCP TypeScript SDK.

faq.question: Does it create a complete server automatically?
faq.answer: No. It provides design guidance, examples, checklists, and an evaluation harness.

faq.question: Can it test an MCP server?
faq.answer: Yes. The included harness can run read-only XML evaluations against stdio, SSE, or HTTP MCP servers.

faq.question: Does it need credentials?
faq.answer: Evaluation with Claude requires an Anthropic API key. Target services may require their own credentials.

faq.question: What security checks are important?
faq.answer: Review commands, remote URLs, headers, secrets, tool permissions, destructive actions, and response data exposure.
